key: D major in the orchestral original; band version transposed
question: What changes when winds rather than an orchestral string section carry the march’s long melody?
intro: The United States Marine Band plays a concert-band arrangement, in a different key from the orchestral original. Compare its wind-led sonority with the orchestral recordings without treating the change of ensemble or repeat scheme as a conductor’s tempo decision.

cues.title: Band, not symphony orchestra
cues.text: This is a concert-band arrangement, not a third orchestral reading. Compare the way winds sustain and articulate the melody with the string-led orchestral versions; do not attribute every difference of colour to the conductor.
cues.evidence: Wikimedia Commons identifies the United States Marine Band and links the official Marine Band MP3. The precise arranger and conductor are not established. The version distinction applies to the entire performance, not an entrance at 0:00.

cues.title: A pronounced withdrawal
cues.text: The first broad melody follows a sharp change of level and texture. Listen for how a wind ensemble connects the longer line after the short march figures, while the recording becomes substantially quieter.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-usmb.txt: strongest boundary at 1:20; relative level falls from −7.3 dB at 1:10 to −22.9 at 1:20, with lower spectral brightness. The report does not separate individual wind instruments.

cues.title: Length is not tempo alone
cues.text: The broad interior repeats its material, occupying much more time than in the two historical orchestral files. The comparison therefore aligns the later march and final trio, rather than forcing this entire span into a misleading one-to-one tempo measurement.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-usmb.txt places the interior around 1:20–3:20, against approximately 1:12–2:08 in Elgar. cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-usmb-trio-repeat.json aligns this file’s 81–139 and 140–199 seconds with median confidence 0.971 and no transposition, supporting the additional traversal. Repeat differences are not reduced to speed.

cues.title: The shared excerpt begins
cues.text: The returning march starts the portion aligned with Elgar and Stock. From here, compare the spacing of the short gestures before the broad tune returns; the matching is provisional, not an assertion of identical orchestration.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-usmb.txt: structural boundary at 3:20 and renewed onset activity. The map aligns Elgar 128–258 seconds with this file’s 200–343 seconds, median chroma confidence 0.964. Only matching features are transposed by two semitones; audio is unchanged.

cues.title: Different key, familiar contour
cues.text: The band version’s pitch level differs from the orchestral recordings. Follow the melody’s contour and phrase length rather than absolute pitch when switching; the player does not retune either recording.
cues.evidence: The band report estimates C major where both orchestral reports estimate D major. More decisively, the shared reprise-and-trio sequence aligns with median confidence 0.964 using transposeB −2; this is feature matching, not a claim about the unidentified arrangement’s printed key signature.

cues.title: A sustained final crest
cues.text: The late broad melody remains at a high recorded level before the closing gestures. Compare that sustained weight with the first, quieter trio span rather than reading the level strip as an absolute loudness comparison with the old discs.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/elgar-pomp-circumstance-1-usmb.txt: loudest five-second windows include 4:50, 5:10, 5:15 and 5:20. Levels are normalised within this file; the decoded duration is 346.0 seconds, including its ending.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US-government sound recording: Commons explicitly applies PD-USGov-Military-Marines to the performance/recording
fields.note: Rule 1, recording-specific US-law basis under 17 USC §105, not worldwide CC clearance. Commons separates Performance/Recording from Composition and attributes the file to a Marine Band official-duty recording with an official .mil source. No CC-NC licence appears in the Commons record or the reviewed official source wording. Marine Band boilerplate says its institutionally distributed recordings ‘may not be distributed for private use and are not for sale’ because appropriated funds are used: this is the agency’s physical-distribution policy, not a non-commercial copyright licence on the government performance. Official web downloads are offered separately. Direct upstream retrieval returned HTTP 403 during this research; the official page’s indexed distribution wording and reader-accessible download instructions were examined, and the file’s recording-specific Commons declaration remains explicit. No claim of worldwide rights or a cleared private arrangement is made.

composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
